chapters.title: Chapter 301 | The Banking Issue
paragraphs: "How can I help?"
Dexter explained the restriction, and she nodded, extending her hand for his identification. "Your name?"
"Dexter."
Dexter paused and the sighed. "Dexter Ashford."
Her fingers stopped. It lasted less than a second, and then her smile returned. "Dexter... Ashford?"
"Yes."

She looked down at the card, then at her screen. Dexter noticed the change but did not immediately attach significance to it. People reacted to the Ashford name for many reasons—admiration, fear, curiosity, sometimes simple surprise that someone carrying it would be waiting in a public queue.
The banker typed for a while. "I see the account."
"Good."
"There are some verification requirements."
"That’s why I’m here."
"Of course." She smiled again. "First, we’ll need confirmation of your current residential address."
Dexter reached into his spatial storage and produced the property documents. Her eyes flickered toward his hand as he placed the house deed and accompanying paperwork on the counter.
"This is the property where I live."
She picked up the deed, read the first page, turned to the second, then back to the first. Dexter waited.
"The address here is different from the address originally attached to your banking profile."
"I moved."
"Yes, I understand. However, the original address is the Ashford estate."
"That’s where I used to live."
"Would you happen to have confirmation of the change?"
Dexter looked at the deed beneath her hand. "You’re holding it."
"We need to establish that the property is actually occupied by you."
He brought out another document, then the household registration information saved on his phone. The banker examined both. "Please wait while I check with verification."

She stood and walked through a door behind the counters. Dexter remained seated. Five minutes passed, then ten. He looked at the clock. He still had time. There was no reason to turn a routine bank visit into an argument.
When the woman returned, she carried a printed form. "Please complete this."

Dexter took the pen and filled it in. Name. Current address. Previous address. Identification number. Occupation. He paused briefly before writing ’Foodsmith and registered hero*l’. The woman watched his pen move, and when he finished, she read the form.
"A foodsmith?"
"Yes."
"Are you employed by an establishment?
"I sell prepared meals through a bakery."
"Which bakery?"
He gave the name and location, and she typed it in. "And your income from hero activities?"
"I haven’t claimed any recent mission earnings."
Her fingers paused again. Dexter saw it this time—the slight movement at the corner of her mouth—but she continued typing before he could decide what it meant.
"We’ll need proof of earnings."

He nodded. That, at least, sounded reasonable. He opened his payment records and showed her the transfers connected to his food sales, along with the sales summaries he had kept. She examined them carefully—too carefully, considering how little information each contained.
"These are individual payments."
"They’re payments for my food."
"Do you have an employment certificate?"
"I just told you I’m not employed by the bakery. I supply it."
"Then perhaps a formal salary statement?"
Dexter looked at her. "I don’t receive a salary."
The banker gave a sympathetic smile. "I understand, sir. Unfortunately, without proof of earnings, we can’t release the funds."
He glanced at the records on the counter. "What are these?"
"Supporting documents."
"Supporting what?"
"Your income declaration."
"Then what additional document do you require?"
"A formal proof of earnings."
Dexter’s expression changed slightly, but the woman kept smiling. For the first time since sitting down, he looked at her without trying to make the interaction easier. "Define formal."
She blinked. "I’m sorry?"

"You’ve asked for proof of earnings. I’ve shown you records of my sales. You’ve asked for proof of residence. I’ve given you the deed and my current registration. Tell me exactly what document you need."
Her eyes shifted toward the door behind her—only for a moment, but Dexter saw it. "Given the size of the balance, further verification is required."
"Then verify it."
"We’re trying to."
"No," he said quietly. "You’re asking the same question in different ways."
The banker’s smile thinned. "Sir, please understand that we have procedures."
"I understood the first four procedures. I complied with all of them."
She folded her hands. "The account contains a substantial amount of money."
"I’m aware of that.
"And these food sales do not account for the entire balance."

Dexter became still. That was a genuine distinction—his bakery earnings and the system’s rebate were not the same thing—but the bank already had the incoming transaction records. Whatever the system had done to deposit the money, the transfer had been accepted and reflected in his account before access was restricted.
He leaned forward slightly. "Then show me the specific transfer under review. Give me the sender details your system recorded and the exact documents required for that transfer."
"I’m not authorized to provide internal verification information."
"You’re authorized to prevent me from accessing my money, but not to tell me what would resolve the restriction?"
"The relevant department will contact you."
"When?"
"I can’t provide a time frame."
Dexter stared at her. The woman looked back with the expression of someone who had reached a sentence she intended to repeat until he left. His patience finally broke.
"I want to speak to your manager."
Several people nearby looked up, and the banker’s eyes sharpened. "There’s no need to raise your voice."
"I said I want your manager."
"Sir, the manager is currently occupied."
"Then tell him a customer is waiting."
"If you continue disturbing other customers—"
Dexter laughed once. There was no amusement in it. "I’ve spent the morning bringing out every document you asked for. Each time I give you one, you invent another reason nothing can be done."
A clerk at the next counter stopped typing, and the banker lowered her voice. "Please calm down."
Dexter glared at the idiot in front of him and then at the Clerk next to the counter and spat.
"Get your fucking manager."

One of the guards near the entrance began walking toward them, and Dexter noticed him without turning. The banker did too, and a trace of confidence returned to her face. "Sir, we’re asking you to cooperate."
"I have been cooperating."
"Please keep your voice down."
"Then stop trying to end the conversation without answering my damn question."

More customers were watching now. A man holding a paper cup lowered it, and someone farther back whispered the Ashford name. Dexter ignored them and kept his eyes on the banker. "Are you refusing to let me speak to the manager?"

Before she could answer, a door opened beyond the counters. A middle-aged man in an expensive suit stepped out, wearing the relaxed smile of someone accustomed to arriving after other people had created a problem and receiving credit for solving it.
"Is there an issue?"
The banker immediately straightened. "Sir, this customer—"

chapters.title: Chapter 302 | Money Or Pride...
paragraphs: A middle-aged man in an expensive suit stepped out, wearing the relaxed smile of someone accustomed to arriving after other people had created a problem and receiving credit for solving it.
"Is there an issue?"
The banker immediately straightened. "Sir, this customer—"
The manager’s smile did not change, but his eyes did. "Of course. Mr. Ashford." He approached with his hands loosely clasped. "I apologize for the delay. Account reviews can be frustrating."
Dexter halved coldly at the Manager’s face.
"Then perhaps you can explain this one."
"Certainly. Let’s discuss it in my office."
Dexter remained seated for a moment as the manager glanced at the documents on the counter. "We can offer you more privacy there and solutions."
Dexter gathered his papers, and the banker looked relieved.

The office was spacious, with a wide desk standing in front of a window overlooking the street. A framed banking license hung on one wall, and on another was a landscape painting expensive enough to feed an ordinary family for years.
The manager gestured toward a chair.
"Please."
Dexter remained standing. "Explain the restriction."
The manager raised his hand and pressed a remote.
"Click!"
The closed the door, and the lock clicked softly. His smile disappeared. The change was so immediate that Dexter even edmired his act.
The man walked behind his desk and sat down—he did not offer an apology, nor did he open the file. Instead, he looked at Dexter with mild irritation.
"You could have saved everyone a great deal of time."
Dexter’s eyes narrowed. "What do you mean?"
"You know how these things work.
"Apparently not."
The manager leaned back. "As you know, this bank is basically owned by your family. You should understand why your account was blocked."

The room became very quiet, and Dexter looked at him as the manager continued. "If you want the account unblocked, you need to accept the family’s invitation. After that, we can do something about it."

For a few seconds, Dexter said nothing. The house deed in his hand suddenly felt ridiculous—the forms, the waiting, the patient explanations. They had known who he was from the moment the banker entered his name. They had simply decided to make him sit there and perform obedience before telling him the price.
"The invitation," he repeated.
The manager opened a drawer and placed a black envelope on the desk. Gold lettering marked its front—the Ashford crest. Dexter stared at it.
"The family wishes to speak with you," the manager said. "This needn’t become unpleasant."
"You froze fifty million dollars to make me attend a conversation."
"I didn’t freeze anything. A restriction was placed on the account because of the untraceable money sent to it. It could belong to someone else and sent to you by mistake. So we need to be careful."
Dexter’s expressionless face glanced at the man. "Have you ever seen someone send 50 million dollars by mistake?"
The man blinked his eyes and chuckled drily. "There’s a first time for everything."
The manager spread his hands. "Look, there’s no need to make things unnecessarily difficult or complicated."
Dexter’s jaw tightened. The fifty million had already become part of those plans, and now the Ashfords were holding it beyond his reach, waiting to see whether his need would bend his spine.
The manager watched his face. "You should be practical, Mr. Ashford."
Dexter slowly lifted his gaze. "Practical."
"Attend. Listen. If there’s a disagreement, resolve it privately. Surely that’s preferable to creating scenes in public." The man tapped the envelope. "They are still your family."
Dexter felt something cold settle beneath his anger. He had heard that sentence used to excuse too many things—hunger, humiliation, punishment, abandonment. Now theft dressed in banking language.
"You wasted my morning," he said.
The manager’s expression sharpened. "We gave you an opportunity to handle this discreetly."
"Yes," Dexter said. "I can see that."
The manager’s eyes hardened. "You seem to believe that shouting changes your position. It doesn’t."

Dexter looked at the envelope again. He could take it, attend, smile across a table at people who had thrown him away and pretend their interest had arrived because they missed him rather than because he had become useful. Then perhaps the account would open.
His breathing slowed, and the manager mistook the silence for consideration. "A sensible decision now would make your life much easier."
Dexter raised his eyes. "No."
The word was quiet, and the manager blinked.
"You have substantial funds in this institution. Are you willing to leave it inaccessible over your pride?"
Dexter’s mouth curved. It was not a smile the manager liked. "You think this is about pride?"
The man said nothing.
Dexter stepped toward the desk. "Tell the family..." His palm settled lightly against the polished surface. The manager looked down. "...it’s not over yet."
Dexter pressed.
"Thump!"

The center of the desk collapsed beneath his hand as fractures shot through the wood, the supports buckled, and drawers burst from their fittings as the entire structure folded inward with a heavy crash.
The manager jerked backward in fear as his chair slammed backwards against the wall. For the first time since entering the office, his expression became honest and was filled with fear.
The black envelope slid through the wreckage and landed near his shoe. Dexter stood amid the settling dust, and slowly withdrew his hands.
The force had gone through the desk and into nothing else.
The manager’s mouth opened, but no words emerged. Outside, hurried footsteps approached, and Dexter gave a cold snort before turning and opening the door.
Two guards stood beyond it. They looked past him at the shattered desk, then at their manager, pale and rigid against the wall.
"Sir?"
The manager swallowed. His gaze met Dexter’s, and a moment passed. Then he said, "Let him leave."
Dexter walked between the guards. The banker at counter six looked up, and whatever she saw on his face made her immediately lower her eyes.
He did not stop as he crossed the lobby, passed the waiting customers, and stepped out into the sunlight.
Behind him, the bank doors closed with a soft, expensive click.

chapters.title: Chapter 303 | Traning Begins
paragraphs: Dexter sat in his vehicle without starting it, his hands resting on the steering wheel. For several moments, he stared through the windshield. Then he laughed under his breath, Fifty million dollars. He has already calculated what he was going to buy with the money but now, it’s seemed it had been just a pipe dream.
The laugh faded as he opened the banking application.
The balance had not changed, neither had the restriction. He took screenshots of the notice, the account balance, and the record of his branch visit before putting the phone down.
He would need them—not to beg the same people again, but to make sure that when he eventually moved against this, he had more than anger.
His fingers tightened around the steering wheel, and the material creaked. Dexter released it immediately and looked at the small mark his thumb had left. Then he leaned back and closed his eyes.
Mira had been right. He had not even reached the cashier before trouble started.
A faint vibration came from his phone. For one unpleasant instant, he expected another message from the bank. Instead, it was Lyra.
She sent a photograph of the egg, this time, there was two more cracks on the egg making six cracks. Under the photograph was a message:
Lyra: ’Look! Its still lazy.’
Dexter stared at it, and a little of the tension left his face as he smiled and typed back: ’It definitely takes after you.’
The response arrived quickly: ’Bully! I’m telling Mira.’
A second message followed: ’Did you eat?’
Dexter looked at the food container on the passenger seat. He had forgotten it.
He opened the lid. The food was still warm inside its insulated wrapping, and for a while he ate in silence, almost forgetting what had happened.
Just enjoying fhe meal Lyra had put into his hands.
He sent a brief message home: ’The bank is taking longer to resolve than expected. I’m safe. Heading to training. I’ll explain when I return.’

He considered adding more, then decided that explaining the whole thing through messages would only leave them worrying without the chance to ask questions properly. Cole’s booking details were already waiting Titan Training Center, two o’clock. Dexter checked the time, it was still a bit early.
He started the vehicle.
The Titan Training Center looked exactly as he remembered—reinforced walls, wide entrance, a steady stream of registered heroes moving through the security checkpoints.
Dexter slowed as he approached the gates. His last visit with Violette rose briefly in his mind. He had come here to test himself.
Today, the task was different, he was training with his new teammates.
Cole stood near the entrance with Gridlock. He noticed Dexter first and raised a hand. "Youre early.
Dexter smiled as he stepped out of the vehicle. "You should disappointed."
"I had a whole speech prepared."
"Save it for Blitz."
Gridlock looked at his watch. "He’s already here."
Dexter raised an eyebrow. "Really?"
"He arrived seven minutes early."
Cole laughed, and Dexter found himself smiling despite the morning. They completed registration and entered the facility. As they walked, Cole glanced at him.
"Everything all right?"
Dexter was quiet for a moment, then said, "Family problems."
Cole’s expression changed slightly. "Do you need to postpone?"
"Nah, it’s nothing I can’t handle."
Cole considered that, then nodded. "All right. But if you wish to head out early, tell me. "
That was a reasonable request.
"No problem."
Cole gave a small nod and they continued walking.
The arena was way larger than the room Dexter had used for his earlier spar.

Several movable partitions stood along its edges, and reinforced floor panels could rise into obstacles while projectors mounted above the walls generated targets and marked areas of danger. A control station overlooked the space behind protective glass.

Blitz was stretching when they entered, Bulwark sat on a bench with his enormous arms folded, and Bullet Spear Man leaned against the wall with his collapsed weapon resting beside him. He looked up when Dexter arrived.
"Thought you’d forgotten."
Dexter glanced at the clock. "We’re early."
"Wasn’t talking about the time."
Cole stepped between the conversation and whatever it might become. "We’re all here. Good.
Gridlock placed a case of training markers on the floor. Blitz straightened. "Are we finally fighting something?"
"After we discuss what we’re doing."
Bulwark made a sound that might have been a laugh, and Dexter looked around the group.
Cole activated a display, and a simple formation appeared above the central table. "Today isn’t a competition to see who can destroy the largest target," he said.
Blitz looked disappointed.
"We know we can fight individually. We need to find out whether we can move together without making each other less effective."

Gridlock nodded, and Cole continued. "I’ll handle the broad calls unless someone sees an immediate danger. Bulwark takes the front when we need a fixed line. Gridlock protects movement and controls access. Blitz scouts, retrieves, and interrupts." His gaze moved to Bullet Spear Man. "You handle ranged pressure and exposed targets." Then Dexter. "You’re our flexible close-range fighter. If a flank collapses, you respond. If we need an opening widened, you take it."
Dexter studied the arrangement. It made sense. It also placed him in a position where restraint would matter as much as speed.
"What’s the first objective?"
"Escort three civilian markers through a damaged street."
Blitz pointed at the display. "Those things?"
Three human-shaped training dummies appeared on the screen. "One cannot move without assistance," Cole said. "Another is slow. The third is mobile but will follow the route the simulation assigns."
"Meaning it might run the wrong way," Gridlock said.
"Exactly."
Bullet Spear Man rolled his shoulders. "And the opposition?"

sentences.text: Dexter sat in his vehicle without starting it, his hands resting on the steering wheel.
For several moments, he stared through the windshield.
Then he laughed under his breath, Fifty million dollars.
He has already calculated what he was going to buy with the money but now, it’s seemed it had been just a pipe dream.
The laugh faded as he opened the banking application.
The balance had not changed, neither had the restriction.
He took screenshots of the notice, the account balance, and the record of his branch visit before putting the phone down.
He would need them—not to beg the same people again, but to make sure that when he eventually moved against this, he had more than anger.
His fingers tightened around the steering wheel, and the material creaked.
Dexter released it immediately and looked at the small mark his thumb had left.
Then he leaned back and closed his eyes.
Mira had been right.
He had not even reached the cashier before trouble started.
A faint vibration came from his phone.
For one unpleasant instant, he expected another message from the bank.
Instead, it was Lyra.
She sent a photograph of the egg, this time, there was two more cracks on the egg making six cracks.
Under the photograph was a message:
Lyra: ’Look!
Its still lazy.’
Dexter stared at it, and a little of the tension left his face as he smiled and typed back: ’It definitely takes after you.’
The response arrived quickly: ’Bully!
I’m telling Mira.’
A second message followed: ’Did you eat?’
Dexter looked at the food container on the passenger seat.
He had forgotten it.
He opened the lid.
The food was still warm inside its insulated wrapping, and for a while he ate in silence, almost forgetting what had happened.
Just enjoying fhe meal Lyra had put into his hands.
He sent a brief message home: ’The bank is taking longer to resolve than expected.
I’m safe.
Heading to training.
I’ll explain when I return.’
He considered adding more, then decided that explaining the whole thing through messages would only leave them worrying without the chance to ask questions properly.
Cole’s booking details were already waiting Titan Training Center, two o’clock.
Dexter checked the time, it was still a bit early.
He started the vehicle.
The Titan Training Center looked exactly as he remembered—reinforced walls, wide entrance, a steady stream of registered heroes moving through the security checkpoints.
Dexter slowed as he approached the gates.
His last visit with Violette rose briefly in his mind.
He had come here to test himself.
Today, the task was different, he was training with his new teammates.
Cole stood near the entrance with Gridlock.
He noticed Dexter first and raised a hand.
"Youre early.
Dexter smiled as he stepped out of the vehicle.
"You should disappointed."
"I had a whole speech prepared."
"Save it for Blitz."
Gridlock looked at his watch.
"He’s already here."
Dexter raised an eyebrow.
"Really?"
"He arrived seven minutes early."
Cole laughed, and Dexter found himself smiling despite the morning.
They completed registration and entered the facility.
As they walked, Cole glanced at him.
"Everything all right?"
Dexter was quiet for a moment, then said, "Family problems."
Cole’s expression changed slightly.
"Do you need to postpone?"
"Nah, it’s nothing I can’t handle."
Cole considered that, then nodded.
"All right.
But if you wish to head out early, tell me.
That was a reasonable request.
"No problem."
Cole gave a small nod and they continued walking.
The arena was way larger than the room Dexter had used for his earlier spar.
Several movable partitions stood along its edges, and reinforced floor panels could rise into obstacles while projectors mounted above the walls generated targets and marked areas of danger.
A control station overlooked the space behind protective glass.
Blitz was stretching when they entered, Bulwark sat on a bench with his enormous arms folded, and Bullet Spear Man leaned against the wall with his collapsed weapon resting beside him.
He looked up when Dexter arrived.
"Thought you’d forgotten."
Dexter glanced at the clock.
"We’re early."
"Wasn’t talking about the time."
Cole stepped between the conversation and whatever it might become.
"We’re all here.
Good.
Gridlock placed a case of training markers on the floor.
Blitz straightened.
"Are we finally fighting something?"
"After we discuss what we’re doing."
Bulwark made a sound that might have been a laugh, and Dexter looked around the group.
Cole activated a display, and a simple formation appeared above the central table.
"Today isn’t a competition to see who can destroy the largest target," he said.
Blitz looked disappointed.
"We know we can fight individually.
We need to find out whether we can move together without making each other less effective."
Gridlock nodded, and Cole continued.
"I’ll handle the broad calls unless someone sees an immediate danger.
Bulwark takes the front when we need a fixed line.
Gridlock protects movement and controls access.
Blitz scouts, retrieves, and interrupts." His gaze moved to Bullet Spear Man.
"You handle ranged pressure and exposed targets." Then Dexter.
"You’re our flexible close-range fighter.
If a flank collapses, you respond.
If we need an opening widened, you take it."
Dexter studied the arrangement.
It made sense.
It also placed him in a position where restraint would matter as much as speed.
"What’s the first objective?"
"Escort three civilian markers through a damaged street."
Blitz pointed at the display.
"Those things?"
Three human-shaped training dummies appeared on the screen.
"One cannot move without assistance," Cole said.
"Another is slow.
The third is mobile but will follow the route the simulation assigns."
"Meaning it might run the wrong way," Gridlock said.
"Exactly."
Bullet Spear Man rolled his shoulders.
"And the opposition?"
"Constructs and projected attacks.
The facility will register hits through these."
Cole distributed small monitoring bands, and Dexter secured one around his wrist.
The band flashed, read his energy, and settled to a dull blue.

Nobody needs to reveal every technique they possess.

chapters.title: Chapter 304 | Training II
paragraphs: They moved into position as the lights changed, and sections of the floor rose, forming a broken street bordered by low walls and damaged building fronts. Three rescue markers appeared behind them.
"Ding!"
The exercise began.
A pale curtain of light swept across the arena, and the ceiling seemed to retreat. In its place appeared a vast, overcast sky above the ruins of an abandoned settlement.
Broken towers rose beyond the street, their upper floors disappearing into drifting mist. Vines covered the walls, and deep claw marks scored the stone beneath Dexter’s feet.

He glanced down. The floor had not truly become stone—when he looked closely, he could see faint threads of light running through it—but the roughness beneath his boots felt real. A gust of wind struck his face, and then a shadow passed overhead.
"Above!" Blitz called.
Dexter raised his head. Three enormous creatures circled between the broken towers. Wyverns.
Their bodies were covered in dark scales, their long necks ending in narrow heads crowned with swept-back horns.
Two powerful hind legs hung beneath their bodies, while hooked claws protruded from the joints of their wings. Each creature was large enough to swallow a man whole.
A translucent display appeared at the edge of the arena.
[COMBAT SIMULATION]
[Enemy Species: Blackscale Wyverns]
[Enemy Strength: Superhuman Realm]
[Objective: Eliminate the hostile creatures and secure the extraction route.]
[Additional Objective: Protect the three injured-party markers.]
Dexter’s gaze sharpened.
This was much closer to the dungeon he had experienced at the Hero Association.

But these wyverns were projections, formed from light and sustained by the arena’s formations, but their attacks would carry controlled force, and the monitoring bands would register injuries according to where and how heavily they were struck. Getting hit would still hurt—enough to discourage carelessness.
Cole lifted his right hand. "Bulwark, front. Gridlock, cover the injured markers. Blitz, watch the rooftops." The others moved. "Dexter, right flank. Spear, left. Keep the center open."

A sharp cry split the air, and one of the wyverns folded its wings and dropped. The creature fell between two ruined buildings like a dark spear, then spread its wings at the last moment. A violent gust swept down the street, scattering projected rubble across the ground.
Blitz disappeared from where he had been standing, and Gridlock thrust his palm forward, raising a translucent barrier before the three rescue markers. Bulwark stepped into the wyvern’s path.
"Come here."
The creature struck. Its claws slammed against his raised forearms, and the floor shook beneath his feet.
Bulwark slid backward nearly a meter, his boots leaving bright streaks across the simulated stone, but his body remained upright. He grinned.
"That’s better."
The wyvern opened its jaws, and orange light gathered deep inside its throat.
"Breath attack!" Dexter shouted.
Bulwark immediately turned his shoulder and shoved upward. The creature’s head jerked aside, and a stream of fire swept across the ruined wall beside them.

Heat washed over Dexter’s face, and even knowing it was artificial, his body reacted to the danger. He moved, lightning flickering around his legs, and in the next instant he was beside the wyvern. His practice saber struck beneath its wing, passing through scales that offered convincing resistance before breaking apart into fragments of light. A bright wound appeared along the creature’s side, and the wyvern screamed and thrashed. Dexter shifted to avoid its tail.
At the same moment, a second wyvern dived toward him.
"Dexter, hold!" Cole called.

Dexter saw the descending claws and pushed off the ground—too late to hear the rest of the instruction. A compressed ball of plasma shot through the space he had just entered. Cole jerked his arm sideways, and the attack veered away and exploded against a ruined tower. White light filled the street, and Dexter landed on a broken ledge.

Below him, Bullet Spear Man thrust his weapon toward the first wyvern’s exposed throat. The spear shot forward with a sharp crack and pierced the creature’s neck. The wyvern burst into scattering fragments of light.
"One down," Bullet Spear Man said.
"Left rear!" Blitz shouted.

The third wyvern had ignored the fighters entirely. It flew low along the street, heading straight toward the injured markers. Gridlock raised a second barrier, and the creature struck it with both feet.

Cracks spread across the translucent surface. Bulwark turned, Dexter dropped from the ledge, and Blitz flashed toward the creature’s head—all three moved at once, and none reached the marker before the barrier broke. A claw swept through the first artificial casualty. Red light flooded the arena.
"Ding!"
[OBJECTIVE FAILED]
The wyverns froze, their bodies dissolving into pale particles while the ruined street remained. For several seconds, the six men stood in silence. Then Blitz turned toward the others.
"Well. That went beautifully."
Gridlock lowered his hands. "I had two attack directions to cover."
"I saw the second one coming," Dexter said.
Cole looked at him. "So did I. That was why I told you to hold."
Dexter glanced at the scorched tower, then back at Cole. "You had a shot."
"Yes."
Dexter exhaled. "That was mine."
Bullet Spear Man rested his weapon against his shoulder. "We still killed one."
Gridlock looked at the extinguished rescue marker. "And lost someone behind us."

The spear fighter did not answer, and Cole walked toward the center of the group. "This is why we needed the session." He looked from one face to another. "We reacted as six individual fighters. Bulwark held the first target, Dexter attacked it, Spear finished it, and then three people rushed the same threat while Gridlock was left handling the consequences."
Blitz raised a finger. "In my defense, I was rushing very quickly."
Nobody laughed, and he lowered the finger. "Fine. Difficult audience."
Cole pointed toward the sky. "They can fly. We can’t treat them like monsters lining up in a corridor."
Dexter studied the ruined buildings, his eyes moving from the rooftops to the narrow passage between them. "Then we stop fighting them in the open."
Cole followed his gaze, and a moment later he smiled. "All right. Tell us."

chapters.title: Chapter 305 | The Training III
paragraphs: They restarted the exercise again.
This time, Bulwark did not wait in the center of the street—he moved toward the narrowest section between two damaged buildings.

Gridlock placed the rescue markers behind a low wall where he could protect them with a smaller barrier, Bullet Spear Man stood several steps to Cole’s left, and Dexter took the opposite side while Blitz climbed onto a broken ledge.
The wyverns appeared, their cries echoing over the ruins.
"Three overhead," Blitz called. "First one descending. Second circling left. Third staying high."
"Let the first come," Cole said.

Bulwark rolled his neck as the diving wyvern spread its wings and struck him. This time, he was ready for the exact force. He caught one of the hooked wing claws and drove his heel against the floor, and the creature’s momentum dragged him backward but only a little.
"Now!"
Dexter moved. He did not leap toward the creature’s head—he cut beneath its wing, forcing it to twist away from the pain registered by the simulation.
That turn exposed the throat, and Bullet Spear Man thrust. His attack struck the wyvern’s neck at an angle that prevented it from releasing its breath, and the creature recoiled.
Above them, the second wyvern descended to help.
"High left," Blitz called.

Cole raised his hand. This time, Dexter stayed low. Plasma shot over his shoulder and struck the second wyvern beneath its chest. Its wings snapped outward, and a violent explosion of light hurled it into the side of a tower. Before it could recover, Blitz appeared on the broken ledge beside it, struck its eye, and vanished.
The creature’s head jerked toward him—that was enough. Cole’s next shot hit the same damaged point, and the wyvern dissolved.
"One," Cole said.
Bulwark tightened his grip on the first creature’s wing. "Would someone like to finish mine?"
Dexter drove his saber through the glowing weakness at the base of its neck. The projection shattered. "Two," he replied.
A shadow covered the street as the last wyvern climbed higher, its throat glowing.
"Move the markers!" Cole snapped.
Gridlock withdrew the frontal barrier and raised two slanted shields over the protected area. Blitz reached the nearest marker, Dexter caught the second, and Bulwark grabbed the third by its harness.
A broad stream of fire struck the street behind them, and heat rolled over the barriers. Gridlock’s face tightened.
"I can’t hold the heat for long!
"Don’t," Cole said. "Drop them on my mark."

The wyvern followed its attack lower—that was its mistake. Bullet Spear Man had already planted his feet, and his spear shot upward, striking the creature at the hinge of its jaw. Its head snapped back, and the flame cut off.
"Drop!"

Gridlock released the shields, and Cole’s plasma attack tore through the opening. Dexter sprang from the top of the low wall, caught the edge of a broken platform with one foot, pushed off, and struck the wounded creature before it could regain height.
His saber flashed across the underside of its neck, and the wyvern came apart around him. Fragments of light drifted down like sparks as Dexter landed.
For a moment, everyone waited. Then a clear tone sounded.
[FIRST WAVE COMPLETE]
Blitz grinned. "That looked much better."
The ground trembled, and new shadows appeared above the towers. Five this time. His grin faded. "Of course."

The second wave forced them to move. The wyverns did not attack together—two remained high, harassing the team with breath attacks, another circled behind the buildings, and the remaining pair repeatedly dived at the front line, trying to force Bulwark away from the protected route.
The projections behaved like living predators. They changed direction when attacked, retreated from bad angles, and sought the weakest point.
At first, the team struggled. Gridlock raised a barrier too close to Bullet Spear Man’s weapon and forced him to cancel a thrust. Blitz moved before announcing it, leaving Cole briefly exposed.

Dexter pursued an injured wyvern farther than necessary and had to retreat when a second creature cut across his return route. But the mistakes became smaller, and more importantly, they began correcting them before the formation collapsed.
"Right side open," Dexter called.
"Covering," Gridlock answered.
"Three seconds," Cole said.
Bulwark ducked, and plasma crossed above him. A wyvern fell.
"Spear, high target!"
"I see it."
"Blitz, don’t chase.
"I’m not chasing." He reappeared beside them. "I was investigating at speed."
Dexter almost laughed, and then claws struck the wall beside his head and he returned his attention to the fight.

By the fourth restart, their calls had become shorter. They no longer explained every movement. Bulwark planted his feet, and the others knew he was about to hold a target. Gridlock lifted two fingers, and Blitz changed his route before a barrier appeared.

Cole’s gathering plasma became a signal Dexter understood without looking directly at him. When Bullet Spear Man aimed past his shoulder, Dexter lowered his stance and trusted the weapon to pass where it was supposed to.
That last part required effort, and the man noticed. His expression changed slightly, but he said nothing.
They kept fighting. During the final run, the simulation added a larger wyvern. Its scales were edged with silver light, and its aura carried the oppressive weight of a peak Superhuman creature.
It emerged from behind the tallest tower with both wings spread, and the smaller wyverns scattered around it.
Blitz looked up. "That one seems unnecessarily enthusiastic."
The great creature roared, and its breath struck the street like a descending furnace.
"Back!" Cole shouted.

They withdrew together. Bulwark protected the slower movement of the markers, Gridlock redirected falling rubble with a barrier, Dexter severed a smaller wyvern’s attack before it reached Cole, and Bullet Spear Man struck another through the wing, forcing it down.

The larger creature landed, stone bursting beneath its claws. A spiked tail whipped toward the group, and Bulwark intercepted it. The impact drove him sideways, and his monitoring band flashed amber. Simulated damage.
"Still standing," he growled.
Dexter saw the movement beneath the monster’s raised wing—a gap. Small. Difficult to reach while the creature could turn freely. He looked toward Cole.
"Can you make it face you?"
Cole’s eyes flicked toward the gap, then back to Dexter. "For how long?"
"Two breaths."
Cole smiled thinly. "You got it!"
